### Summary

`XdsServer` in `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` does not apply `RBACPerRoute` overrides from matching Route or VirtualHost resources. When a trusted xDS control plane supplies a broad top-level ALLOW policy and a stricter override, `XdsServer` ACKs the resources but evaluates the RPC under the top-level policy.

### Details

### Override parser lookup uses the override message type

`parseOverrideFilterConfig()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts:225-257 looks up FILTER_REGISTRY using the override message type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts#L225-L257

`setup()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts:167-173 registers the filter only under the top-level RBAC type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts#L167-L173

The lookup returns null even though the registered entry contains `parseOverrideRbacConfig()`, and server.ts silently skips the override.

### Override maps are keyed by type URL instead of filter name

`overrideConfigMaps` in server.ts:99-102 is documented as keyed by HTTP filter name, but server.ts:169-174 stores each map under `filterConfig.typeUrl`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L99-L102

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L169-L174

Route overrides are later looked up by their `typed_per_filter_config` key, which is the `HttpFilter.name`. An ordinary key such as rbac therefore misses the stored map.

### VirtualHost overrides are not read

`handleRouteConfigurationResource()` in server.ts:225-249 reads `route.typed_per_filter_config` but never reads `virtualHost.typed_per_filter_config`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L225-L249

When no override reaches the RBAC interceptor, rbac-filter.ts:125-155 evaluates the broader top-level policy.

### Proof of concept

Set:
```
GRPC_XDS_EXPERIMENTAL_RBAC=true
```

Run `XdsServer` with a protected unary handler.

Have the ADS control plane deliver a Listener containing an RBAC HTTP filter named rbac with a top-level ALLOW-any policy:

```
name: rbac
typed_config:
  "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC
  rules:
    action: ALLOW
    policies:
      allow-any:
        principals: [{ any: true }]
        permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Deliver a matching non-forwarding route with this override:

```
typed_per_filter_config:
  rbac:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute
    rbac:
      rules:
        action: DENY
        policies:
          deny-any:
            principals: [{ any: true }]
            permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Invoke the protected unary method without credentials.

Expected: The route-specific DENY policy rejects the RPC before the protected handler runs.

Observed: `XdsServer` ACKs the resources, retains the top-level ALLOW policy, and runs the protected handler.

```
Listener and RouteConfiguration: ACKED
gRPC status: OK
handler invocations: 1
response: PROTECTED_SECRET_RECORD_RBAC_OVERRIDE
```

### Impact

Users of `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` who are using RBAC-based authentication with override configurations may unintentionally accept some requests that should be rejected.

### Summary

The **JRuby** implementation of msgpack (`msgpack` gem, `java` platform — pure Java decoder under `ext/java/`) sizes containers directly from the element count written in the message header, with **no cap at all**: no equivalent of the C unpacker's `SHRT_MAX` clamp (since 1.7.3) and none of the buffered-bytes cap that commit c8d42d8 added for CRuby in 1.8.6. A single 5-byte message decides how much memory a JVM process tries to allocate:

* `array32` header declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` elements → `new IRubyObject[0x7FFFFFFF]` (~8 GiB of reference slots) attempted immediately → `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit`.
* Counts *below* the VM's max-array-size but above available heap (e.g. 5×10⁸ with a 512 MiB heap) produce a **real allocation attempt** — `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` — the JVM genuinely tries to take the memory before failing.
* `str32`/`bin32` headers declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` bytes do the same via `readBytes(size)` → `new byte[size]`.
* Below the failure threshold there is a **silent band**: one streaming unpacker fed only an `array32` header with count 2×10⁷ (5 wire bytes, zero elements) grows used heap **+78 MiB immediately**, no exception (`each` swallows the underflow), and the footprint stays elevated after `Unpacker#reset` + full GC. Linear in declared count (~4 B/element); nothing bounds it — not delivered bytes, not a per-container cap.

Only counts ≥ 2³¹ are refused (a clean `MessagePack::UnderflowError` from `getUnsignedInt()`), and only **maps** are safe (`consumeHash` grows per element instead of pre-sizing). Verified on the released gem `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12 / OpenJDK 25, 2026-10-30 — i.e. **unfixed in the current release**. Proposed fix mirrors c8d42d8: cap initial allocation by bytes actually buffered and grow as data arrives; read strings in bounded chunks instead of allocating the declared length up front.

### Details

### 1. The four dispatch arms, and which pre-allocate (line numbers at tag v1.8.6 — current release; `ext/java` has no commits after it)

| header | dispatch ([Decoder.java](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java)) | behaviour on the declared count | measured (released 1.8.6-java, Xmx512m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `array32` `\xdd` | [:296](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L296) → [`consumeArray(int size)` :139-145](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L139-L145) | `new IRubyObject[size]` **immediately**, before reading any element | count `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "Requested array size exceeds VM limit"; count 5×10⁸: OOME "**Java heap space**" (real allocation attempt); count 2×10⁷: **+78 MiB, silent** |
| `str32` `\xdb` | [:294](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L294) → [`consumeString` :129](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L129) → [`readBytes(int size)` :186-190](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L186-L190) | `new byte[size]` **immediately** | len `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "array size exceeds VM limit" |
| `bin32` `\xc6` | [:269](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L269) → same `consumeString`/`readBytes` | same | len `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "array size exceeds VM limit" |
| `map32` `\xdf` | [:298](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L298) → [`consumeHash(int size)` :147+](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L147) | **no pre-allocation** — inserts per element, underflows on first missing byte | count `0x7FFFFFFF`: no exception (swallowed), no large allocation |

The only guard is [`getUnsignedInt()` :88-94](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L88-L94): counts with the top bit set (≥ 2³¹) raise `MessagePack::UnderflowError: Size too large (limited to 2**31 for the Java version)`. That bounds the *value* but leaves the entire positive band `(available heap, 2³¹)` unbounded — and that band is where real allocation attempts happen.

### 2. Contrast with the C implementation (same repo)

The CRuby unpacker has had a per-container cap since 1.7.3 (`INITIAL_BUFFER_CAPACITY_MAX = SHRT_MAX`) and, since [c8d42d8](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/commit/c8d42d8) in **1.8.6**, additionally caps initial size by bytes actually buffered ("an element needs at least one byte…"). Strings on C are bounded too (`read_raw_body_cont` allocates `min(remaining, buffered)`). The Java decoder has **neither generation of cap** — it is strictly behind the CRuby behaviour this repo already considers correct enough to ship.

### 3. Silent retention + mechanism control (measured 2026-10-30, released gem)

One `MessagePack::Unpacker` per process, fed only a header (`"\xdd" + [count].pack('N')`), zero elements; heap = `Runtime.total_memory - free_memory` after `GC.start` on both sides:

| declared count | used heap before → after | delta | exception? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000,000 | 26.4 → 31.1 MiB | +4.7 | none (`each` swallows the underflow) |
| 5,000,000 | 53.3 → 74.0 MiB | +20.7 | none |
| 20,000,000 | 51.3 → 129.3 MiB | **+78.0** | none |

Mechanism control: after the feed, `Unpacker#reset` + three `GC.start` cycles left used heap at **+79.4 MiB above baseline** (2×10⁷ arm) — the elevation is *not* unpacker-held state; it is JVM heap already spent on header-declared allocation and not returned. Either way the process footprint grows per attack and stays grown; the peak cost is paid synchronously during parsing regardless of GC behaviour afterwards. (Honest scope note: this is unbounded **allocation**, not a memory leak.)

### 4. Why JVM makes availability impact worse than the CRuby analogue

In CRuby, allocation failure raises `NoMemoryError`/fails inside one worker process. In a JVM, an OOME raised on the parser thread can land anywhere in the host application's shared runtime — long-lived JRuby servers (Rails, Logstash-class pipelines, JDBC apps) share heap across all threads and connections; a single crafted message can destabilize or kill the whole JVM, not just the request. The silent band means no exception at all is even required to spend memory.

### 5. Not claimed / scope

* **Fluentd is NOT affected** (and this report deliberately does not involve it): Fluentd ships CRuby-only — CI pins `engine: cruby`, gemspec requires ruby >= 3.3 while JRuby 9.4 implements Ruby 3.1 semantics, and there are zero JRUBY guards in lib/. This is an upstream msgpack-ruby report only.
* Maps (`map32`) do not pre-allocate — measured; the class applies to `array32`/`str32`/`bin32`.
* Counts ≥ 2³¹ are cleanly refused — measured; no claim there.
* Older java-gem releases were not individually probed; `<= 1.8.6` means "every release up to the current one carries this code".

### Proof of concept

Verified on the **released gem** `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12.0, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, Linux x86-64 (artifacts in `evidence_186_recheck/`). Always run with a small `-Xmx` so oversized requests fail fast instead of wrecking the box.

### Setup

```console
$ curl -fsSLO https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/jruby/jruby-dist/9.4.12.0/jruby-dist-9.4.12.0-bin.tar.gz
$ tar xzf jruby-dist-9.4.12.0-bin.tar.gz && export PATH=$PWD/jruby-9.4.12.0/bin:$PATH
$ jruby -S gem install msgpack --no-document      # resolves the java-platform gem: "msgpack (1.8.6 java)"
```

### 1. Header shapes (fresh process per arm, `-Xmx512m`)

```console
array32 count=0xFFFFFFFF       -> MessagePack::UnderflowError: Size too large (limited to 2**31 for the Java version)
array32 count=0x7FFFFFFF       -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
array32 count=500000000        -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space   # real allocation attempt
str32   len=0x7FFFFFFF         -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
bin32   len=0x7FFFFFFF         -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
map32   count=0x7FFFFFFF       -> no exception, no large allocation (consumeHash grows per element)
```

Each payload is five bytes, e.g. `"\xdd" + [count].pack('N')` fed to `MessagePack::Unpacker#feed_each`. Scripts: `jr_probe.rb`, `jr_probe_extra.rb` (attached in kit).

### 2. Silent band — retention from one header (Xmx1g)

```console
$ for n in 1000000 5000000 20000000; do jruby -J-Xmx1g jr_one.rb $n; done
count=  1000000 heap 26.4 -> 31.1 MiB (delta 4.7)   | no exception (underflow swallowed)
count=  5000000 heap 53.3 -> 74.0 MiB (delta 20.7)  | no exception (underflow swallowed)
count= 20000000 heap 51.3 -> 129.3 MiB (delta 78.0) | no exception (underflow swallowed)

$ jruby -J-Xmx1g jr_reset_control.rb 20000000
count=20000000 heap base=49.9 after_feed=129.3 (delta 79.4) after_reset_gc=129.3 (retained_vs_base 79.4)
```

A streaming server that keeps one unpacker per connection (the pattern any socket-fed msgpack service uses) pays this per connection with five wire bytes each and produces no exception, no log line.

### 3. Fix verification path

Apply the C-side idea from c8d42d8: in `consumeArray`, cap the initial array by bytes actually buffered (an element needs ≥ 1 byte) and grow as elements arrive; in `readBytes`/`consumeString`, read in bounded chunks instead of allocating the declared length up front. Then re-run this PoC: the silent band should track delivered bytes, and oversized declarations should raise `UnderflowError`-class errors without touching multi-GiB allocations. msgpack-ruby CI runs jruby-9.4/truffleruby, so a patch is verifiable as-is; I can prepare one against `ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java`.

### Impact

**Type.** Uncontrolled resource consumption driven by *declared* sizes rather than delivered bytes — CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling), precisely CWE-1325 (Independent Resource Usage Limiting Not Applied). Availability only; no confidentiality/integrity impact, no code execution.

**Who is impacted.** Any JRuby application that feeds untrusted msgpack to `MessagePack.unpack`/`Unpacker` — the java-platform gem's whole user base (JRuby-based services, log/RPC pipelines, JVM polyglot stacks using this gem). For them: remote OOM of a shared-heap JVM from a 5-byte message, or silent heap spend below the exception band.

**Severity.** Proposed **High / 7.5**, `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` — remote, trivially crafted, default settings, process death; same metric string as the accepted fluentd OOM family (e.g. GHSA-h3xv-5jpx-r4j2) and as this repo's own C-side analogue (reported separately, patched at 1.8.6). If triage weighs the platform scope (java gem only), lower framings read against that — we flag it honestly; the maintainers' call on scope shouldn't delay the patch.

**Relationship to the C-side report.** Same flaw class, different implementation and fix state: CRuby's pre-allocation was capped by c8d42d8 (released 1.8.6, separate advisory with affected `<= 1.8.5`, patched `1.8.6`). This JRuby variant is **unfixed in 1.8.6** and needs its own patch + CVE. Cross-reference both ways once filed.

**What this is not.** Not a Fluentd issue (Fluentd is CRuby-only — CI pins cruby, gemspec ruby >= 3.3 vs JRuby's Ruby 3.1 semantics); no fluentd advisory should carry this. Not a memory leak (measured: footprint elevation persists after reset+GC without retained objects). Not exploitable via maps or counts ≥ 2³¹ (both measured safe/cleanly refused).

### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode`, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that are not valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

- labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. `xn--google-` decodes to `google`;
- labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

`Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so for `https://xn--google-.example.org/` it displays the host `google.example.org`, while `#host`, `#normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI use `xn--google-.example.org`. An attacker who controls a domain can therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control. Applications that compare the result of `to_unicode` against a list of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, is not affected. `to_ascii` and `normalized_host` are not affected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.0.0, the first version with the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, when that implementation is in use. It is fixed in 2.9.1, where such labels are returned unchanged, as with libidn.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation.
- Don't make security decisions on `display_uri` or `to_unicode` output. Compare hosts using `normalized_host`.

### Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode` decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that contain characters which change how text is displayed without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width characters, and other invisible format characters. `Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so it can display a host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to a different host. For example, the host of `http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/` is displayed as `abc`, U+202E, `moc.com`, and the override makes everything after `abc` render right to left.

Parsing, `host`, `normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that show `display_uri` to users (link previews, chat and email clients, admin interfaces) can be used to make a malicious domain look like a trusted one.

- In the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, all such characters are decoded, including those that IDNA's nameprep profile prohibits.
- In the native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, libidn rejects most of them, but not characters added to Unicode after version 3.2, such as U+061C and U+2066–U+2069.

### Affected Versions

The pure-Ruby IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.0.0. The native IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.5.2, when `to_unicode` began accepting characters unassigned in Unicode 3.2. It is fixed in 2.9.1 for both implementations, where such labels are returned unchanged.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation. This reduces the affected characters to those added since Unicode 3.2.
- Check displayed hosts for bidirectional and invisible characters (e.g., `/[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\p{Default_Ignorable_Code_Point}]/`) and fall back to `normalized_host` when one is present.

### Credits

Reported by @andrewstellman.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

### Impact

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` takes time quadratic in the number of nested dot segments in a path (e.g., `"/" + "a/" * n + "../" * n`, which for n = 3 is `/a/a/a/../../../`), because it removes one dot segment per pass over the whole path. `URI#normalize`, `URI#normalized_path`, `URI#==`, `URI#===` and `URI#join` all call it. Normalizing, comparing or joining a URI taken from user input can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. On 2.9.0, normalizing a 34 KB path takes about 3.5 seconds on MRI Ruby 4.0, and the cost grows with the square of the path length.

This affects every Ruby implementation, including MRI Ruby 3.2 and later. `URI.parse` by itself is unaffected, as is code that never normalizes, compares, or joins URIs from untrusted sources.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects all versions of Addressable prior to 2.9.1. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

### Workarounds

- Limit the length of URIs taken from user input before calling `normalize`, `==` or `join` on them. Web servers often limit request lines to about 8 KB, which keeps the cost to about 150 milliseconds per call on typical hardware, but URIs from other sources (request bodies, headers such as `Location`, stored data) may not be limited.
- Reject paths with many dot segments before normalizing them.

### Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security, who also suggested the single-pass approach used in the fix.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

## Summary The `@astrojs/solid-js` renderer wraps named slot content passed to Solid components in an `` element, and writes the slot name into its `name` attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing `"` could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page. For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request: ```astro import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.jsx'; const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab');
…
 ``` rendered with a Solid component that renders a slot by name: ```jsx export default function Tabs(props) { return
{props[props.active]}
; } ``` would output a `tab` value such as `x">` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true: - The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name. - The Solid component is hydrated with a `client:*` directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its `name` attribute. - The Solid component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means accessing slot props by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template. This is the `@astrojs/solid-js` counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in `astro` core. ## Affected versions `@astrojs/solid-js` >= 0.2.0, <= 7.1.1. ## Patches Fixed in `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component. ## Credits Reported by @manus-pi.

### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates using the `*` (explode) modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators (e.g., `{/segments*}`, `{.ext*}`, `{;params*}`, `{?query*}`) generate regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character, matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator, and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part of the expression was never reached. This issue was originally reported in #364 by @ebenoist in 2019 but insufficiently investigated.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is only exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. MRI Ruby 3.2 and later are not affected: their regular expression engine memoizes backtracking, so these patterns still match in linear time. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected either. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|

### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates that put several variables in one expression generate regular expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than `+` and `#` (e.g., `{/owner,repo,ref}`, `{.a,b}`, `{a,b,c}`, `{;a,b,c}`). The values are joined by an optional separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the `+` or `#` operators and many variables (e.g., `{+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}`). A failing match is exponential in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g., `{+a}{+b}{+c}` or `{a}{b}{c}`), which are polynomial in the input length.

When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. A three-variable path template such as `http://example.com/repos{/owner,repo,ref}` needs about 2 KB of input to occupy a thread for many seconds.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. The second form, many-variable `+` and `#` expressions, is also exploitable on MRI Ruby 3.2, which does not memoize a regular expression that contains possessive quantifiers, and 2.9.0 generates those for these operators. It is also exploitable on TruffleRuby 40.0, whose regular expression engine falls back to backtracking for them. MRI Ruby 3.3 and later are not affected by any form, because they memoize those regular expressions too. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected by the other two forms. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates with several variables in one expression, or with several expressions next to each other.

### Summary

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` resolves some paths containing `..` segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs above the root before any other `..` is resolved, the segments that later `..` segments should remove are instead kept: `/../../public/x/../../secret` normalizes to `/public/x/secret` instead of `/secret`. `URI#normalize`, `URI#join`, `URI#==` and `URI#===` all use this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a request for a path outside the allowlist.

### Details

`normalize_path` in 2.9.0 (`lib/addressable/uri.rb`) removes dot segments by repeating a set of rewrites until nothing changes. On each pass it finds the first `/segment/../` pair with `RULE_2B_2C`, then replaces every textual copy of that pair in the path with `/`:

```ruby
pair = normalized_path.match(RULE_2B_2C)
...
regexp = "/#{Regexp.escape(parent.to_s)}/\\.\\./|"
regexp += "(/#{Regexp.escape(current.to_s)}/\\.\\.$)"
...
mod ||= normalized_path.gsub!(Regexp.new(regexp), SLASH)
```

When the first pair found is `/../../`, where the "segment" is itself `..`, every `/../../` in the path is replaced with `/`. That includes copies later in the path, where each `..` should have removed the segment before it. For `/../../public/x/../../secret`:

- RFC 3986 §5.2.4 drops the two leading `..` segments, which can't go above the root, then removes `x` and `public`, giving `/secret`.
- 2.9.0 replaces both copies of `/../../` with `/` in one step, giving `/public/x/secret`.

Paths where an ordinary `/segment/../` pair comes first, such as `/a/../../b/c/../../d`, are resolved correctly.

This was introduced in 2.2.5. Versions 2.0.0 through 2.2.4 and earlier versions resolve these paths correctly. It is fixed in 2.9.1, which replaces the rewrite loop with a single pass that correctly follows RFC 3986 §5.2.4.

### Proof of concept

```ruby
require "addressable/uri"
require "uri"

url = "http://example.com/../../public/x/../../secret"

# Addressable's normalized path, compared with RFC 3986 resolution by Ruby's URI library
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path
puts URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path

# join and == use the same normalization
puts Addressable::URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url) == Addressable::URI.parse("http://example.com/public/x/secret")

# An allowlist check on the normalized path passes, but the request reaches /secret
def allowed?(url) = Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path.start_with?("/public/")
puts allowed?(url)
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.0:

```
/public/x/secret
/secret
/public/x/secret
true
true
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.1:

```
/secret
/secret
/secret
false
false
```

### Impact

This is an interpretation conflict (CWE-436) between Addressable and other RFC 3986 resolvers, which could lead to path traversal past an allowlist (CWE-22). An application is affected when it does both of these:

- makes an access decision on a path normalized or joined by Addressable, such as "only paths under `/public/` may be proxied" or "only these redirect targets are allowed";
- sends the original, unnormalized URI to a component that resolves dot segments itself, such as an HTTP client, a proxy, a web server or a browser.

An attacker may be able to bypass a check by exploiting behavioral differences between URI parsers. Impact from this is application-dependent. Applications that use Addressable's normalized form for both the check and the request are unaffected, as are applications that reject paths containing `..` segments.

As a work-around for unpatched versions, before making access decisions on a path, either reject any containing `..` segments, including percent-encoded forms such as `%2e%2e`, or use the same normalized value for both the check and the request.

### Impact
Active Storage's `VideoPreviewer`, `VideoAnalyzer` and `AudioAnalyzer` run `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on a blob's contents without restricting the input format, so FFmpeg selects a demuxer by probing the file. A blob created through a direct upload keeps the content type the client declared, so a client can store an HLS playlist under a `video/*` or `audio/*` type. When that blob is previewed or analyzed, the `hls` demuxer opens the `file://` segments that the playlist names, and the preview image or the stored metadata could disclose a local media file that the application process can read and whose path the attacker knows.

Applications that accept uploads from untrusted users and generate video previews, or analyze video or audio attachments with FFmpeg, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases limit the formats FFmpeg may open to common audio and video containers, configured by the new `config.active_storage.ffmpeg_allowed_formats` setting. Files in other formats no longer preview or receive media metadata; the Active Storage CHANGELOG names some of them and shows how to add a format to the list.

### Workarounds
Applications that cannot upgrade can stop Active Storage from running FFmpeg on uploaded files by removing `ActiveStorage::Previewer::VideoPreviewer` from `config.active_storage.previewers`, and `ActiveStorage::Analyzer::VideoAnalyzer` and `ActiveStorage::Analyzer::AudioAnalyzer` from `config.active_storage.analyzers`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:

### Summary

While `@hono/node-server` waits for the Hono application to handle a WebSocket upgrade request, the socket has no error listener. If the client resets the TCP connection during that time, the resulting `ECONNRESET` is emitted as an unhandled `'error'` event and the process terminates.

### Details

The upgrade handler awaits the application before attaching any listener to the socket. When middleware on the upgrade path does asynchronous work, such as an authentication lookup, a connection reset in that window has no handler. If a global `uncaughtException` handler swallows the error, the pending upgrade is never released and its entry is retained for the lifetime of the process.

The fix attaches error and close listeners to the socket before calling the application, releases the pending upgrade when the socket closes, and skips the handshake on a destroyed socket.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can terminate the server process with a single connection by sending a WebSocket upgrade request and resetting the connection before the application has responded. Where the crash is suppressed, repeated requests grow the heap.

This affects applications that enable WebSocket support in `@hono/node-server` and run asynchronous middleware or handlers on the upgrade path.

### Summary

`@hono/node-server` passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as `/` and then resolves `..` segments. A request for `/admin\secret` or `/public\..\admin/secret` reaches the application as `/admin/secret`. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.

### Details

A raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.

The fix responds with `400 Bad Request` to a request whose path contains a raw backslash, for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, absolute-form request-targets and WebSocket upgrades. A percent-encoded backslash and a backslash in the query string are still accepted.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route that a reverse proxy, load balancer or WAF in front of the application blocks by path.

This affects applications served by `@hono/node-server` behind a front component that makes path-based decisions and forwards a backslash unchanged. Access control inside the Hono application, such as middleware on `/admin/*`, runs on the rewritten path and is not affected.

## Summary

Loofah restricts `href` and `xlink:href` on certain SVG elements to same-document references. Two elements escaped the restriction:

- `<textPath>`: `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF` listed it in lowercase as `textpath`, but the HTML5 parser names the element `textPath` inside `<svg>`, so the check never matched on the HTML5 path.
- `<mpath>`: absent from `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so its references were never restricted on either path.

`rails-html-sanitizer` reuses this safelist in its `PermitScrubber`, so it is affected too.

## Impact

An external `href` or `xlink:href` on `<textPath>` or `<mpath>` survives sanitization. Firefox fetches the URL when rendering the content, which leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent, and referrer, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. Chrome and WebKit do not fetch external references on these elements. The impact is a network request to an attacker-chosen URL, not script execution.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied SVG, directly or inside HTML, with Loofah's default allowlist or with `rails-html-sanitizer` with SVG elements permitted are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `javascript:` or `vbscript:` URI whose scheme is split by a numeric character reference without a trailing semicolon, followed by a character that `allowed_uri?` strips, such as a space or tab. A browser ends the reference at that character and reads `javascript&#x3a alert(1)` as `javascript: alert(1)`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` strips control characters and whitespace before it decodes numeric character references. Removing the character that ends a semicolon-less reference lets the reference run on into the following text, so `&#x3a alert` decodes as `&#x3aa` (U+03AA) instead of a colon, and no scheme is detected. The same applies to decimal references and to references that encode a scheme letter, as in `&#x6a\tavascript:alert(1)`.

Loofah's default `sanitize()` path is **not** affected, because Nokogiri decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue affects only callers of the public `allowed_uri?` string-level helper that pass it HTML-encoded strings.

## Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with `Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` and then render the approved value into an `href` or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to cross-site scripting. `Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri?` re-exports the same helper.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @manus-pi.

## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css` rejected any property whose top-level Crass tokens included a `:url` or `:bad_url`, and left `url` out of the allowed CSS functions. Both checks ran only against the first parse of the `style` attribute. A sanitized `style` attribute could make a viewer's browser issue a request to an attacker-chosen URL. `list-style` fetches on render with no interaction, `cursor` on hover. That leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent and access timing, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. No script survives sanitization and the attacker cannot read the response, so the request itself is the whole impact.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied HTML with Loofah's default allowlist and display it to other people are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Reported by NotAFlightRisk through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting.

cves.summary:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 sanitizer restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

The default safelist allows the elements in `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so no configuration change is required.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3. Applications that cannot upgrade should run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time.

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `data:` URI whose mediatype is written with the HTML5 named character reference `/` in place of the solidus. Loofah reads that mediatype as malformed and falls back to the allowed `text/plain`, while a browser decodes the reference and reads the same URI as `text/html`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` decodes HTML entities with `CGI.unescapeHTML`, which handles numeric character references but not HTML5 named character references. `/` therefore survives normalization, so the mediatype carries no `/`, fails the MIME grammar, and falls back to the allowed `text/plain` under the WHATWG rule for a malformed mediatype.

`:`, `/`, `	` and `
` are the only named character references in the HTML5 table that decode to characters that change how a URI parses (U+003A, U+002F, U+0009 and U+000A; there is no named reference for U+000D), so this closes the set.

Loofah's default `sanitize()` path is **not** affected, because Nokogiri decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue affects only callers of the public `allowed_uri?` string-level helper that pass it HTML-encoded strings.

## Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with `Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` and then render the approved value into an `href` or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to cross-site scripting. `Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri?` re-exports the same helper.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @ngpestelos.

## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 scrubbers could emit output that a browser parses into different markup, allowing mutation XSS. Nokogiri < 1.19.5 did not escape `<` and `>` in attribute values. When the output contained certain MathML, a browser treated markup inside an allowed attribute as live HTML. The `:strip` scrubber is affected in every browser. The `:prune` and `:escape` scrubbers are affected in WebKit browsers such as Safari.

Not affected: Loofah's HTML4 API (including `Loofah::Helpers.sanitize`), the `:whitewash` scrubber, rails-html-sanitizer's default configuration, and JRuby.

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3, or upgrade Nokogiri to >= 1.19.5.

cves.summary:
### Summary

Every `pg_hba.conf` generated by the pgEdge Control Plane begins with a hard-coded block of `trust` entries covering Unix-socket and loopback connections. Any operating-system account that can reach the Postgres socket or the loopback interface on a database host can authenticate as any Postgres role, including the superuser, without presenting a credential.

### Details

The generated file opens with the following six entries:

```
local   all         all                     trust
host    all         all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    all         all     ::1/128         trust
local   replication all                     trust
host    replication all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    replication all     ::1/128         trust
```

Postgres evaluates `pg_hba.conf` top-down and stops at the first matching rule. Because these entries are emitted at the top of the file, they also pre-empt every rule below them — including entries supplied by an operator through the `pg_hba_conf` field of a database node specification, which are appended lower in the file and are therefore never reached for local or loopback connections.

Both supported orchestrators emit these entries, but exposure differs by deployment model:

* **systemd** — the database runs on a shared multi-user host. Any local account
  on that host can connect as the Postgres superuser. This is the
  higher-severity case and the one the CVSS score below reflects.
* **Docker Swarm** — the Unix socket and the loopback interface belong to the
  Postgres container, so reaching these entries requires code execution inside
  that container. Publishing the Postgres port to the host does not change this:
  such connections are not seen by Postgres as originating from `127.0.0.1` or
  `::1`, so they do not match the entries above. The practical exposure is
  correspondingly narrower.

An operator who verifies their own deployment can confirm the issue by inspecting the generated `pg_hba.conf` on a database node for the entries above.

### Impact

An unprivileged local operating-system account on an affected database host obtains full control of every Postgres database on that host: read of all data, modification or destruction of all data, and any action available to a Postgres superuser. Under the systemd orchestrator this converts any local account into a database superuser with no additional prerequisites.

### Affected versions

pgEdge Control Plane v0.1.0 through v0.10.1, inclusive.

### Patches

Fixed in **v0.11.0**. Generated `pg_hba.conf` files no longer contain `trust` entries, and operator-supplied local authentication rules take effect. Upgrading to v0.11.0 or later is the recommended and, on v0.9.0 and later, the only complete remedy.

### Workarounds

The available mitigation differs by version, and no mitigation is complete on current releases.

**v0.1.0 – v0.8.1.** An operator could take the authentication files out of Patroni's control entirely: copy the generated `pg_hba.conf` and `pg_ident.conf`, edit the copies, and point the `hba_file` and `ident_file` settings at them through node-level `postgresql_conf`. This is effective but must be repeated per instance, including for every node added afterwards.

**v0.9.0 – v0.10.1.** The above no longer applies. API validation rejects the `hba_file` and `ident_file` settings, and entries supplied through the `pg_hba_conf` specification array are appended below the hard-coded block rather than overriding it, so they do not take effect for local or loopback connections. The only partial mitigation available is to restrict the Unix socket: set `unix_socket_permissions` to `0700`, or to `0770` with the intended accounts placed in the `postgres` group. **This closes the socket path only. No supported configuration closes the loopback path on these versions.** Operators on v0.9.0 – v0.10.1 should upgrade to v0.11.0.

### Impact

An unauthenticated caller able to reach the query endpoint could exhaust database and server resources with ordinary, inexpensive requests.

The keyword-search arm read the entire corpus on every request and rebuilt an in-memory BM25 index from it, so the cost of serving a query scaled with the size of the source table rather than with the size of the result set. Each request cost the server and the tenant's database far more than it cost the caller to make, which makes this a materially more effective denial-of-service lever than flooding the endpoint with ordinary requests. The amplification factor grows with corpus size, so the largest deployments are the most exposed.

Hybrid search was enabled by default and configured per pipeline rather than per request, so a caller could not opt out of the keyword arm and an operator could not leave it available to some requests but not others.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, whose query endpoint is reachable by an untrusted party. The endpoint required no authentication and applied no rate limiting.

In `1.0.0`, `internal/database/search.go:130` built the corpus query with no `LIMIT`:

```go
query = fmt.Sprintf(`
    SELECT ...
    FROM %s%s`,
    tableIdent,
    filterClause)
```

`FetchDocuments` accepted no limit parameter at all, so neither a caller nor the orchestrator had any way to bound the read.
`internal/config/loader.go:197` defaulted `HybridEnabled` to true, and `internal/server/middleware.go:37` applied only logging, panic recovery and optional CORS.

### Patches

**Fixed in `2.0.0`. Upgrade to `2.0.0` or later.**

Reads are capped by a new per-pipeline `search.bm25_max_documents`, defaulting to 10000, plumbed through `SearchBackend.FetchDocuments` and applied as a parameterised `LIMIT`. There is deliberately no unlimited value: a non-positive setting is rejected at configuration load time rather than silently treated as unbounded.

Requests that reach the cap are logged, because keyword recall is partial at that point and an operator should not have to infer it. A new `disable_hybrid` request field lets a caller skip the expensive arm per query, and can only ever turn it off.

**After upgrading, review the default `search.bm25_max_documents` value of 10000 against the size of your corpus.** A cap far below corpus size silently reduces keyword recall.

### Workarounds

Place the server behind an authenticating, rate-limiting reverse proxy.

Setting `hybrid_enabled: false` on each pipeline removes the keyword arm and with it the unbounded read, at the cost of keyword recall. This is the only mitigation available without a proxy.

Neither is a substitute for upgrading.

### Impact

An unauthenticated remote caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The query API relayed the text of a provider error straight to the caller. That text carried the upstream provider's own message, and providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected when authentication fails — so a failing provider call published a fragment of the operator's key. A caller who can reach the endpoint can cause such a failure and read the result.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, whose query endpoint was reachable by an untrusted party. The endpoint carries no authentication in the affected versions.

The disclosed material authenticates to a **third-party provider account** rather than to pgEdge software, which is why the severity carries Scope: Changed.

`v1.0.0:internal/server/handlers.go:121` relayed `err.Error()` to the client when pipeline execution failed. `parseError` in
`v1.0.0:internal/llm/openai/client.go` produced that error by two routes, and both disclose:

```go
var errResp ErrorResponse
if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &errResp); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("API error (status %d): %s", resp.StatusCode, string(body))
}
return fmt.Errorf("API error (status %d): %s", resp.StatusCode, errResp.Error.Message)
```

The first branch interpolates the entire unparsed response body. The second returns the provider's own message, which for OpenAI quotes the `sk-proj-` prefix and the final four characters of the submitted key.

### Patches

**Fixed in `2.0.0`. Upgrade to `2.0.0` or later.**

The fix adds `internal/safeerr` and stops provider error text reaching API clients.

**Upgrading does not undo the disclosure, and this needs action beyond upgrading. Rotate any LLM provider credential that was configured on an affected version while the endpoint was reachable by an untrusted caller**, particularly if that provider was rejecting the key at the time. A fragment already disclosed stays disclosed.

### Workarounds

Place the server behind a proxy that rewrites 5xx response bodies, or terminate provider errors before they reach the API surface. Keeping provider credentials valid, so that no authentication failure is produced, also avoids the disclosure in practice.

None of these removes the underlying defect, and none is a substitute for upgrading.

cves.summary:
### Impact

Documents belonging to one caller could be returned to another. Where an application passes a customer or tenant identifier as a search filter, that scoping could be defeated by ordinary concurrent traffic. **No injection and no malformed input are required** — normal load is enough.

The BM25 keyword index was a single per-pipeline object shared by every request. A request cleared it, refilled it from its own filtered corpus and then searched it, taking a separate lock for each step rather than holding the sequence as a unit. Concurrent requests therefore interleaved, and a search could run against a corpus that a different request's filter had populated.

**Who is affected:** any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at `1.0.0` or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, that serves concurrent queries — most acutely those relying on a search filter to separate tenants or customers. The query endpoint is unauthenticated in the affected versions (`internal/server/middleware.go:37` applies logging, panic recovery and optional CORS only), so both the party whose results leak and the party receiving them are anonymous remote callers.

### Patches

**Fixed in `2.0.0`. Upgrade to `2.0.0` or later.**

The index is now built per request rather than shared. The regression is pinned by `TestSearch_ConcurrentRequestsDoNotShareKeywordIndex` in `internal/pipeline/orchestrator_test.go`.

**Upgrading does not tell a developer whether or not their application affected, and needs action beyond upgrading.** If a consuminag application scopes results by tenant, treat responses served under concurrent load on any affected version as potentially having included another tenant's documents. **Affected responses cannot be identified from the server's own logs**, so there is no retrospective check available.

### Workarounds

Set `hybrid_enabled: false` on the pipeline, which skips the keyword arm and with it the shared index. Callers can also pass `disable_hybrid` per request, which can only ever turn the arm off.

Neither is a substitute for upgrading.

cves.summary:
### Impact

An unauthenticated caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The library's own health handler pings every configured provider using the operator's real credential and returns the resulting error text verbatim. Providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected, so a failing ping published a fragment of
the key.

**The endpoint is unauthenticated by default.** `authorize()` returns
true immediately when the consuming application sets no `Authorize` hook,
so `GET /v1/health` is reachable by anyone who can reach the listening
port unless the consumer opted in to authentication.

**Who is affected:** any application embedding pgedge-go-llm-lib at
`0.1.0` or `0.1.1` that exposes the bundled HTTP proxy without setting an
`Authorize` hook. Both affected versions are released tags and resolve
through the public Go module proxy.

The disclosed material authenticates to a **third-party provider
account** rather than to pgEdge software, which is why the severity
carries Scope: Changed.

Evidence at `v0.1.1`: `llm/proxy/handlers.go:296` (`handleHealth`
returning `err.Error()` in `ProviderHealth.Error`), `llm/proxy/proxy.go:247`
(`authorize()` defaulting to permit), and `llm/proxy/proxy.go:350`
(`writeError` writing the error with no redaction).

### Patches

**Fixed in `0.2.0`. Upgrade to `0.2.0` or later**, which redacts
credentials from provider error messages unconditionally. The fix adds
`llm/internal/redact`, with a follow-up anchoring word boundaries, and is
pinned by tests in that package.

**Note the version.** There is no `0.1.2` — it was never cut, and some
earlier material named it in error. `0.2.0` is the first fixed release.

**Upgrading does not undo a disclosure that already happened. Rotate any
LLM provider credential configured on an affected version** where the
proxy was reachable without an `Authorize` hook, particularly if a
provider was rejecting that key at the time.

### Workarounds

Set an `Authorize` hook on the proxy, which closes the unauthenticated
route to the health endpoint. Restricting network access to the listening
port limits who can reach it. Neither removes the underlying disclosure
for a caller who does reach the endpoint.

### Impact
An authenticated attacker can call the Autocomplete API with the configured endpoint as a substring to request another server-side route.

### Patches
The problem has been patched in 9.23.0 and pre-release version 10.0.0-beta.4. The regex verifying the endpoint has been anchored to forbid substring injection.

### Workarounds
Use `SharpFormAutocompleteRemoteField::setRemoteCallback()` instead of `SharpFormAutocompleteRemoteField::setRemoteEndpoint()`.

### Impact

An authenticated attacker can instantiate any class in the PHP application by using the `embed_key` parameter across multiple API endpoints. The instantiation is performed by the Laravel container. As a result, the `__construct()` method of the class is called and all constructor dependencies are resolved. The attacker cannot specify parameter values and cannot call any arbitrary method.

### Patches

The problem has been patched in 9.23.0 and pre-release version 10.0.0-beta.4. An additional check was added to verify that `embed_key` is a class extending `SharpFormEditorEmbed` before any instantiation.

### Workarounds

No known workarounds.

cves.summary: ## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in Aspire. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected applications and components. Aspire Dashboard's unauthenticated NotFound route can permit telemetry deletion in both standalone and AppHost-hosted deployments. In standalone deployments using browser-token authentication, it can also expose the browser token. ## Announcement Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/526 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** Critical - **Score:** 9.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N` - **Weakness:** CWE-862 ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** Any supported OS - **Architectures:** x64, Arm64 ## Affected Packages ### Standalone Aspire Dashboard Package | Affected version | Patched version | --- | --- Aspire Dashboard | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 Both 13.6.3 and 13.6.4 contain the unauthenticated NotFound route. ### Aspire Dashboard SDK packages Package | Affected version | Patched version | --- | --- [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-musl-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.linux-musl-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.osx-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-x64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 [Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-arm64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk.win-arm64) | < 13.6.5 | 13.6.5 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? Aspire Dashboard releases through 13.6.4 are affected, whether deployed independently or launched by an Aspire AppHost. For an AppHost using Dashboard SDK packages, check the resolved Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk package versions against the affected ranges above. If the AppHost selects a CLI-bundled Dashboard or a custom Dashboard path, check the version of that Dashboard instead. Aspire ships independently of .NET; installing a .NET runtime or SDK update does not replace the Dashboard. ### How do I fix the issue? Update Aspire Dashboard to version 13.6.5 or later. Neither 13.6.3 nor 13.6.4 is a fixed upgrade target. For container deployments, explicitly set the Dashboard image to `mcr.microsoft.com/aspire/dashboard:13.6.5` and recreate or redeploy the container. Replace older version tags and nightly image references, including those in generated Docker Compose or Kubernetes manifests, with this fixed stable image. Updating AppHost package references alone does not replace an image reference in an existing deployment manifest. For an AppHost using Dashboard SDK packages, update any explicit Aspire.Hosting.AppHost version, including a central package version, to 13.6.5 or later. If that reference is supplied implicitly by Aspire.AppHost.Sdk, update the SDK reference to 13.6.5 or later instead. Restore and rebuild the AppHost, verify that its resolved Aspire.Dashboard.Sdk packages are 13.6.5 or later, and restart the AppHost to run the updated Dashboard. If your AppHost selects a CLI-bundled Dashboard or a custom Dashboard path, update the Dashboard in that selected bundle or location to 13.6.5 or later and restart the AppHost. Updating AppHost package references alone does not replace that Dashboard. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue in the Aspire repository at https://github.com/microsoft/aspire. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. An Improper Authentication vulnerability in the Apache Doris Frontend (FE) meta service allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to access internal metadata service endpoints.

The affected endpoints relied on client-supplied node information for authentication without providing sufficient authentication of the requesting party. Under certain network configurations, a remote attacker may be able to bypass the intended access control and access internal FE metadata interfaces, potentially exposing sensitive cluster information.

This issue affects Apache Doris: from 2.0.0 through 2.0.*, from 2.1.0 through 2.1.*, from 3.0.0 through 3.0.*, from 3.1.0 through 3.1.*, from 4.0.0 before 4.0.8, and from 4.1.0 before 4.1.4. Versions 1.2.x and earlier are not affected by this header-trust vulnerability.

Users are recommended to upgrade to a fixed release (4.0.8 or 4.1.4), which fixes the issue.

The Rename wp-login.php to anything you want plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to time-based SQL Injection via 'log' (Username) Parameter in all versions up to, and including, 2.0.1 due to insufficient escaping on the user supplied parameter and lack of sufficient preparation on the existing SQL query. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to append additional SQL queries into already existing queries that can be used to extract sensitive information from the database. WordPress core applies wp_unslash() to the 'log' POST value before dispatching the wp_login_failed action, stripping magic-quotes backslash escaping and allowing a raw single quote to reach the plugin's handler unimpeded.
